paragraphs.context: superior tone that teachers dressed in nice red business suits
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mrs. Billups sounds polite, but she thinks these children cannot learn or remember as well as other students.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Billups says the class was studying the letter B and that she always starts with basic work. She says these children need the same lessons again and again because she thinks they cannot remember information like other students. Her polite voice also sounds superior.

paragraphs.context: smell freshly sliced lemons and see citrus-toned musical notes
paragraphs.mainIdea: Music makes Melody imagine lemon smells and colored notes in her mind. These are feelings from the song, not real lemons or notes.
paragraphs.simple: Melody loves the song “Elvira,” but she cannot explain this feeling to Mrs. V. When the song plays, Melody imagines fresh lemons and colored music notes in her mind.

paragraphs.context: Songs floated through me and stayed. Lullabies, mixed with the soft smells
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody experiences music as colors, smells, pictures, and feelings, not only as sound.
paragraphs.simple: Music stays inside Melody and gives her more than sound. Songs bring colors, smells, pictures, and feelings into her mind. This is a normal part of how she experiences music.

paragraphs.context: Those pieces always seem to be bright blue as I listen
paragraphs.mainIdea: Beethoven’s music makes Melody think of bright blue and fresh paint. The music is not really blue and does not really smell.
paragraphs.simple: Melody’s mother plays loud Beethoven music. When Melody hears it, the music makes her think of bright blue and the smell of fresh paint. The music is not really blue and does not really smell.

paragraphs.context: Jazz to me sounds brown and tan, and it smells like wet dirt
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jazz makes Melody think of brown and tan colors and wet dirt. Her father likes jazz, but her mother does not.
paragraphs.simple: Melody’s father likes jazz and sometimes puts it on instead of her mother’s music. Melody experiences jazz as brown and tan and as the smell of wet dirt. Her mother dislikes jazz, which may be one reason her father plays it.

paragraphs.context: When I started seeing the colors, I knew she was good
paragraphs.mainIdea: The colors Melody sees are part of how she experiences music in her mind.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. Lovelace plays music to help the class settle down. She changes to music the students like. Melody knows the playing is good when the music begins to give her strong green colors in her mind.

paragraphs.context: Classical music is softly seeping from her new iPod. I hear soft purple
paragraphs.mainIdea: The music gives Melody a soft purple feeling in her mind. She is not really hearing a color.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is working while classical music plays softly. The music gives her a gentle purple feeling in her mind. She is describing her experience of the sound, not a real color.

paragraphs.context: Her body tends to move on its own agenda, with feet sometimes kicking
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody’s body often moves without her choosing the movement, almost as if it follows its own plan.
paragraphs.simple: Melody’s body often moves without her choosing it. Her feet may kick and her arms may move suddenly, sometimes hitting nearby things. Saying her body has its own agenda means it seems to follow its own plan.

paragraphs.context: It’s like I live in a cage with no door and no key
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody feels trapped because her mind has a lot to say, but her body makes speaking and moving very hard.
paragraphs.simple: Melody likes the other children in H-5, but she feels that no one is really like her. She feels trapped because her mind is active while her body and speech limit her. The cage is an image for that feeling.

paragraphs.context: The rest of my body is sort of like a coat with the buttons
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody says most of her body does not work together the way she wants, but her thumbs work very well.
paragraphs.simple: Melody says her thumbs work very well, even though most of her body does not obey her easily. She compares her body to a coat buttoned in the wrong holes: the parts are there, but they do not work together correctly.

paragraphs.context: Country is lemons—not sour, but sugar sweet and tangy
paragraphs.mainIdea: Country music makes Melody think of sweet, fresh lemons. The lemons are part of how the music feels in her mind.
paragraphs.simple: Melody loves country music. In her mind it feels like sweet, fresh lemon flavors and smells, not sour lemons. She is using lemons to describe the feeling the music gives her.

paragraphs.context: It’s like the light has been clicked off. She cries a lot
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jill seems to close herself off and become hard to reach. The light and store-dummy images are not meant as real things.
paragraphs.simple: Jill is quiet and has difficulty moving. When Sydney appears, Jill seems to withdraw and stop responding. The light being switched off and the store mannequin are images showing how hard it is to reach her emotionally.

paragraphs.context: Music, and the colors it produced, flowed around her as easily as her clothing
paragraphs.mainIdea: The colors are Melody’s mental response to music, not colors coming out of the sound.
paragraphs.simple: Mrs. V sometimes plays different kinds of music. Melody experiences the music and its colors as flowing around Mrs. V. The colors are part of Melody’s mental response to sound.

paragraphs.context: The music was sounding orangey and yellowish as I listened
paragraphs.mainIdea: Music gives Melody orange-yellow colors and a light lemon smell in her mind.
paragraphs.simple: Melody is listening to country music and feels happy while watching Ollie. The music gives her orange and yellow colors and a faint lemon smell in her mind. These sensations come from how she experiences music.

paragraphs.context: our school began something called “inclusion classes.” I thought that was funny
paragraphs.mainIdea: The school calls these classes “inclusion,” but Melody notices that she has spent much of her life being left out.
paragraphs.simple: Melody gets an electric wheelchair and starts “inclusion classes.” She finds the name strange because she has often been left out before. The classes are meant to let students like her learn and spend time with students called “normal,” but Melody questions what “normal” means.

paragraphs.context: But I guess it’s perfect for a kid like you
paragraphs.mainIdea: Claire’s words sound polite, but she is treating Melody as different and less important.
paragraphs.simple: Claire comments on Melody’s device and says it is perfect for “a kid like you.” The words may sound friendly, but Claire’s tone and the look she shares with Molly show that she is putting Melody down.

paragraphs.context: I hear no beautiful colors. I smell no lovely aromas
paragraphs.mainIdea: Music usually gives Melody colors and smells. Here she feels none of them, showing how upset and empty she feels.
paragraphs.simple: At the airport Melody hears dull music, but unlike usual, it gives her no beautiful colors or smells. She sees only darkness. The missing sensations show how deeply upset and empty she feels.

paragraphs.context: The only color I heard was gray
paragraphs.mainIdea: Gray describes the dull, sad feeling the music gives Melody. She is not really hearing a color.
paragraphs.simple: After Melody changes into dry clothes, soft radio music plays. She says the only color she hears is gray. Gray describes the dull, sad feeling the music gives her.

paragraphs.context: would never be smart enough to see inside of me
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody privately makes fun of the doctor’s judgment because he cannot see how much she understands.
paragraphs.simple: Melody privately mocks Dr. Hugely because he judges her intelligence without understanding her inner mind. She imagines the zoo and compares him to a smelly elephant. Her smile comes from this private joke, which the adults do not understand.

paragraphs.context: I’ve been packed for ten years
paragraphs.mainIdea: Mr. Dimming does not mean his suitcase has really been packed for ten years. He means he has wanted this trip for a very long time.
paragraphs.simple: Mr. Dimming says he has been “packed for ten years.” He does not mean a suitcase has stayed packed that long. He means he has wanted one of his teams to reach the Washington finals for many years and has been ready for the trip.

paragraphs.context: I have lots to say and just one thumb to say it with
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody has many thoughts and words inside her, but her body gives her only a very limited way to express them.
paragraphs.simple: Melody has a great many thoughts and words inside her mind. Writing them will take time because her body gives her very limited ways to communicate. Her thumb is one of the few body parts she can control well.

paragraphs.context: She probably has mountains of stuff to say
paragraphs.mainIdea: “Mountains of stuff to say” means Melody has a very large amount she wants to communicate.
paragraphs.simple: Miss Gordon explains that the other students have always been free to speak. Melody has had to stay silent even though she has many thoughts. “Mountains of stuff to say” means she has an enormous amount she wants to communicate.

paragraphs.context: Mom and I can sometimes talk without words
paragraphs.mainIdea: Melody and her mother understand many feelings and needs without spoken language because they know each other so well.
paragraphs.simple: Melody and her mother often understand each other without spoken words. A point or look can have different meanings, and her mother knows Melody well enough to understand them. She can also sense Melody’s feelings and help her relax.
